title: Internet, Browsers & E-mail
summary: Internet history and structure, browsers vs search engines, URL/DNS, e-mail mechanics (To/CC/BCC, SMTP/POP3/IMAP) and India's e-banking rails (UPI, NEFT, RTGS). Full forms and the browser-vs-engine trap are asked every year.

subtopics.title: Internet, WWW, URL and DNS
subtopics.concept: The **Internet** is a worldwide network of networks. It grew out of **ARPANET** (1969). The **World Wide Web** is one service on the Internet: linked web pages, invented by **Tim Berners-Lee** in 1989 at CERN. A **URL** is the address of a page. **DNS** turns a name like ssc.gov.in into a numeric IP address.

tricks.title: Internet vs WWW
tricks.body: The **Internet** is the hardware network of cables, routers and servers. The **WWW** is the content service of linked pages on top of it. The Internet is older (1969). The Web is 1989.

example.q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
steps: The Web is the service of linked pages.
It was created in 1989 at CERN.

tricks.title: DNS is the phonebook
tricks.body: DNS turns names into numbers. It never assigns IPs (that is DHCP) and never sends mail (that is SMTP). Any line that says 'converts domain names into IP addresses' means DNS.

example.q: What does DNS do?
steps: Look for the words name and IP address.
Name to number is the phonebook job.
example.answer: It resolves domain names into IP addresses.

mistakes.wrong: Treating WWW and the Internet as the same thing.
mistakes.right: The Internet is the network. The WWW is one service that runs on it.

mistakes.wrong: Saying DNS assigns IP addresses.
mistakes.right: DHCP assigns addresses. DNS resolves names to IP addresses.

mistakes.wrong: Dating the Internet to 1989.
mistakes.right: 1989 is the Web (Berners-Lee). ARPANET was 1969.

mistakes.wrong: Calling HTML a programming language.
mistakes.right: HTML is a markup language. It describes the page.

mistakes.wrong: Reading HTTP as the secure protocol.
mistakes.right: HTTPS is the secure, encrypted one.

subtopics.notes:
### Internet and the Web
The **Internet** is a worldwide **network of networks**. Millions of computers and phones connect through it and swap data.

- It grew out of **ARPANET**, a 1969 project of the US Department of Defense.
- The first two ARPANET nodes were at **UCLA** and **Stanford**.
- **TCP/IP** became its standard protocol suite on 1 January 1983.

The **World Wide Web (WWW)** is a **service that runs on the Internet**. It is a set of linked pages that you read in a browser. **Tim Berners-Lee** invented it in **1989** at **CERN**. E-mail, FTP, VoIP and streaming are other services on the same Internet.

> **Tip:** Internet is the road system. The Web is one kind of traffic on it. The Internet is older (1969); the Web came later (1989).

### Parts of a URL
A **URL (Uniform Resource Locator)** is the address of one page or file. Read it from left to right.

| Part | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Protocol | HTTPS | The rules used for the talk. HTTPS is the secure, encrypted version. |
| Subdomain | www | The host prefix. |
| Domain | ssc.gov.in | The name of the server. |
| Top-level domain (TLD) | .in | The ending. It shows the type or country. |
| Port | 443 | The door number on the server. |
| Path | /exams/ | The folder on the server. |
| File | index.html | The exact page. |

### Common domain endings
| Ending | Meaning |
|---|---|
| .com | commercial |
| .org | organisation |
| .edu | education |
| .gov | government |
| .in | India |

### DNS, DHCP and ISP
Three helpers make a connection work. Each has one job.

| Helper | Job |
|---|---|
| **ISP** (Internet Service Provider) | Sells you the connection. Examples: Jio, Airtel, BSNL. |
| **DNS** (Domain Name System) | Turns a domain name into an IP address. It is the phonebook of the Internet. |
| **DHCP** | Assigns an IP address to your device. |
| **Web server** | Stores pages and sends them to browsers. |

An **IP address** is the number that machines use. IPv4 has four blocks, each from 0 to 255. One example is 142.250.183.14.

> **Watch:** DNS resolves names. DHCP assigns addresses. Exams swap these two on purpose.

### What happens when you open a page
1. You type a URL in the browser.
2. **DNS** finds the IP address of that domain.
3. Your request travels over **TCP/IP** to the **web server**.
4. The server sends the page back.
5. The browser draws the page from its HTML.

Every DNS, URL or ISP question is one stop on this trip.

### Small facts that repeat
- **Bandwidth** is how much data a link can carry. It is measured in bps, Kbps or Mbps.
- **Broadband** is always-on, high-speed access, such as fibre, DSL, 4G or 5G.
- **VoIP** (Voice over Internet Protocol) carries phone calls over the Internet.
- A **website** is a set of related pages under one domain.
- A **web portal** gathers many services on one page.

patterns.name: Internet vs WWW and ARPANET history
patterns.howToSpot: The words 'The Internet is', 'WWW was invented by', 'the year of ARPANET', or a statement that mixes the Internet with the Web.
steps: Match the Internet with ARPANET, 1969.
Match the WWW with Berners-Lee, 1989, CERN.
Remember the Web is a service on the Internet.
Reject any option that treats the two words as equal.
patterns.why: The two dates and the two names are the only facts asked.

example.q: The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 by:
steps: 1989 is the Web, not the Internet.
The Web came from CERN.
example.answer: Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. The Internet is older, from ARPANET (1969).

patterns.name: URL anatomy
patterns.howToSpot: A URL is given and one part is asked: protocol, domain, country code or path. Or the full form of URL.
steps: Split the URL at the slashes.
The start up to :// is the protocol.
The name right after it is the domain.
Everything after the domain is the path.
patterns.why: Each part of a URL has one fixed position.

example.q: In https://www.mysite.in/exams/ssc.html, the domain name is:
steps: https is the protocol.
/exams/ssc.html is the path.
What is left is www.mysite.in.

patterns.name: DNS, DHCP and ISP roles
patterns.howToSpot: 'DNS converts ___ to ___', 'which server assigns IP addresses', 'who provides the Internet connection'.
steps: Find the verb in the question.
Convert or resolve a name means DNS.
Assign an IP address means DHCP.
Provide the connection means ISP.
patterns.why: Each helper has one job, and options swap the jobs.

example.q: The server that converts a website name into its IP address is the:
steps: The job is name to IP address.
That is DNS, not DHCP.

patterns.name: Internet full forms and firsts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Full form of HTTP, HTML, URL, ISP, VoIP' or a pair where one word of the expansion is changed.
steps: Recall the full form word by word.
Compare it with each option.
Reject options with swapped words like 'Hyper Transfer Text'.
Remember HTML is a markup language.
patterns.why: One changed word makes the option wrong.

example.q: The full form of HTML is:
steps: H stands for HyperText.
M and L stand for Markup Language.
example.answer: HyperText Markup Language. It is a markup language, not a programming language.

patterns.name: Domain endings (TLD)
patterns.howToSpot: A domain such as .edu, .gov or .org is given and you must name its type. Or the reverse.
steps: Look at the last part of the domain.
Match it to its meaning.
Check the country code .in for India.
patterns.why: Each TLD has one standard meaning.

example.q: A website whose address ends in .gov most likely belongs to:
steps: The ending is .gov.
.gov means government.

patterns.name: Order of steps to open a page
patterns.howToSpot: 'What happens first when you type a URL?' or 'arrange these steps'.
steps: Start with the URL typed in the browser.
Next comes the DNS lookup.
Then the request goes to the web server.
Last, the browser shows the page.
patterns.why: The IP address must be known before a request can be sent.

example.q: After you type a URL, the browser first asks which service for the server's IP address?
steps: Names are turned into IP addresses by DNS.
This happens before the request is sent.

revision: Internet = network of networks, from ARPANET (1969). WWW = linked pages, Berners-Lee, 1989, CERN.
TCP/IP became the Internet standard on 1 January 1983.
URL = protocol + subdomain + domain + TLD + port + path + file.
DNS: name to IP. DHCP: gives an IP. ISP: sells the connection.
TLDs: .com commercial, .org organisation, .edu education, .gov government, .in India.
HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol. HTML = HyperText Markup Language. VoIP = calls over the Internet.

subtopics.title: Browsers, search engines, downloading and uploading
subtopics.concept: A **browser** is the program that fetches and shows web pages, such as Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari and Opera. A **search engine** is a website that finds pages, such as Google, Bing, Yahoo and DuckDuckGo. **Download** means server to your device. **Upload** means your device to a server.

tricks.title: Browser is the car, engine is the GPS
tricks.body: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari and Opera are browsers, the program you install. Google, Bing, Yahoo and DuckDuckGo are search engines, the websites you visit inside a browser.

example.q: Which of these is a web browser: Google, Chrome, Yahoo, Bing?
steps: Google, Yahoo and Bing are search engines.
Chrome is the program that opens pages.

tricks.title: Ctrl-letter map
tricks.body: T is a new Tab. W closes the tab. D is a Bookmark (Drop a pin). H is History. J is the downloads list. N is a new window, and Shift+N makes it incognito. F5 refreshes.

example.q: Which shortcut reopens a closed tab?
steps: Ctrl+T opens a new tab.
Adding Shift with T brings back the closed one.

tricks.title: Up or down
tricks.body: **Upload** sends a file up to the server. **Download** brings it down to you. The direction is always relative to your machine.

example.q: Saving an e-mail attachment to your PC is called:
steps: The file moves from the server to your PC.

mistakes.wrong: Calling Google a browser or Chrome a search engine.
mistakes.right: Chrome is the browser. Google is the search engine you use inside it.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing up Ctrl+H and Ctrl+J.
mistakes.right: Ctrl+H is History. Ctrl+J is the downloads list.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking cookies are viruses.
mistakes.right: Cookies are passive text files. They are a privacy issue, not malware.

mistakes.wrong: Believing incognito hides you from the ISP.
mistakes.right: Incognito only forgets history and cookies on your device.

mistakes.wrong: Reading upload and download from the server's side.
mistakes.right: Judge the direction from your own device.

subtopics.notes:
### Browser or search engine
A **browser** is a program on your device. It fetches and shows web pages.

- Browsers: **Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox, Safari, Opera**.
- Internet Explorer is retired.

A **search engine** is a website. It keeps an index of the web and finds pages for your words.

- Search engines: **Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo**.

> **Watch:** Google is a search engine. Chrome is a browser. Exams put Google among browsers on purpose.

### Web words
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Webpage | One document, written in HTML |
| Website | A set of related pages |
| Home page | The opening page of a site |
| Portal | One site that bundles many services, such as news, mail and shopping |
| Hyperlink | A link that jumps to another page |

**HTML** is HyperText Markup Language. It builds the page. Hyperlinks join the pages.

### What the browser keeps
| Tool | What it keeps |
|---|---|
| **History** | Every page you visited |
| **Bookmarks** | Pages you saved for a quick return |
| **Cache** | Copies of pages and pictures, so revisits load faster |
| **Cookies** | Small text files a site stores, for logins, preferences and tracking |

Cookies are **not viruses**. They are passive text files. The worry is privacy.

**Incognito (private) mode** forgets history and cookies when you close the window. It is good for shared computers. It does **not** hide you from websites or the ISP.

### Browser shortcuts
| Key | Job |
|---|---|
| Ctrl+T | New tab |
| Ctrl+W | Close tab |
| Ctrl+Shift+T | Reopen the closed tab |
| Ctrl+N | New window |
| Ctrl+Shift+N | New incognito window |
| Ctrl+D | Bookmark the page |
| Ctrl+H | History |
| Ctrl+J | Downloads |
| F5 or Ctrl+R | Refresh |
| Ctrl+F5 | Hard refresh |
| Ctrl+F | Find on the page |
| Ctrl+L or Alt+D | Go to the address bar |
| Ctrl+Enter | Adds the www prefix and .com ending |
| Ctrl + plus, minus, 0 | Zoom in, out, reset |
| F11 | Full screen |
| Ctrl+S, Ctrl+U, Ctrl+P | Save page, view source, print |

> **Tip:** H is for History. J is the Just-downloaded list. The two are often swapped in options.

### Download, upload and streaming
- **Download:** a file moves from a server **to your device**. Songs, PDFs and apps are examples.
- **Upload:** a file moves from **your device to a server**. Attaching a form or posting a video are examples.
- **Streaming:** you play the data as it arrives, without saving the whole file first.

The direction is always seen from **your** machine.

### Searching well
Type keywords, not full sentences. These tricks narrow the results.

| Trick | Effect |
|---|---|
| "exact phrase" | Finds the words together |
| minus sign, as in -word | Removes a word |
| site:ssc.gov.in | Searches only that site |
| OR | Widens the search |

The engine ranks pages by relevance. It does not check whether they are true.

patterns.name: Browser vs search engine
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a browser or a search engine?' or an odd-one-out list of Chrome, Firefox, Google and Safari.
steps: List the browsers: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, Opera.
List the engines: Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo.
Pick the name from the group the question asks for.
patterns.why: Google planted among browsers is the classic trap.

example.q: Which of the following is a web browser?
steps: Bing and Google are search engines.
Chrome is an installed program that opens pages.

patterns.name: Browser shortcut recall
patterns.howToSpot: 'Shortcut to open a new tab, history, downloads or bookmark', with Ctrl+H and Ctrl+J swapped in the options.
steps: Recall the letter: T tab, N window, D bookmark, H history, J downloads.
Add Shift for the incognito or reopen versions.
Watch for Excel, where Ctrl+D means fill down.
patterns.why: One letter decides each shortcut.

example.q: The shortcut that opens the downloads list in Chrome is:
steps: Downloads is the J key.
Ctrl+H opens History instead.

patterns.name: Download, upload, cache and cookies
patterns.howToSpot: 'Downloading means', 'what does the cache store', 'cookies are ___'.
steps: Check the direction of the file first.
Cache means copies kept for speed.
Cookies are small text files, not viruses.
patterns.why: Each word has one plain definition.

example.q: Receiving a file from a web server to your computer is called:
steps: The file moves toward your device.
That direction is download.
example.answer: Downloading. The opposite direction is uploading.

patterns.name: Incognito and privacy features
patterns.howToSpot: 'Incognito mode ___', 'private browsing saves ___'. Sort what is forgotten from what is not hidden.
steps: Recall that history and cookies vanish on closing.
Recall that websites, the office network and the ISP still see you.
Bookmarks you make stay.
patterns.why: Incognito cleans your device, not the network.

example.q: Which statement about Chrome's Incognito mode is TRUE?
steps: It forgets history and cookies after closing.
It does not hide the visit from the ISP or the website.
example.answer: Browsing history and cookies of that window are deleted when it closes.

patterns.name: Search operators
patterns.howToSpot: A search box example with quotes, a minus sign, site: or OR, and a question on its effect.
steps: Quotes keep words together.
A minus sign removes a word.
site: limits to one website.
OR widens the search.
patterns.why: Each symbol changes the search in one fixed way.

example.q: Which search text restricts results to the website ssc.gov.in?
steps: The site: operator limits results to one website.
It goes before the domain.

patterns.name: Web terms: webpage, website, portal
patterns.howToSpot: 'A collection of related pages is', 'the opening page of a site is', 'a site bundling news and mail is'.
steps: One document is a webpage.
A set of pages is a website.
The opening page is the home page.
A site with many services is a portal.
patterns.why: The words differ by size and purpose.

example.q: A collection of related web pages under one domain is called a:
steps: One page is a webpage.
Many related pages together are a website.

revision: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, Opera are browsers. Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo are search engines.
Ctrl+T new tab, Ctrl+W close tab, Ctrl+Shift+T reopen tab, Ctrl+N window, Ctrl+Shift+N incognito.
Ctrl+D bookmark, Ctrl+H history, Ctrl+J downloads, Ctrl+F find, F5 refresh, Ctrl+F5 hard refresh.
Cache = copies for speed. Cookies = site text files (privacy, not viruses).
Download = server to you. Upload = you to server. Streaming = play as it arrives.
Search tricks: quotes for an exact phrase, minus to exclude, site: to limit, OR to widen.

subtopics.title: E-mail: structure, To/CC/BCC and protocols
subtopics.concept: **E-mail** sends messages between accounts on mail servers. An address is username@domain, and **@** separates the two. **CC** copies are visible to all. **BCC** copies are hidden. **SMTP** sends mail. **POP3** downloads it to one device. **IMAP** keeps it on the server and syncs all devices.

tricks.title: CC vs BCC
tricks.body: **CC** is a Carbon Copy that everybody sees. **BCC** is Blind, so To and CC receivers cannot see the blind list.

example.q: The receiver of a mail can see the addresses in which fields?
steps: To and CC are shown to all.
BCC is hidden.

tricks.title: SMTP sends, POP picks, IMAP in-sync
tricks.body: **S**MTP = **S**end (outgoing). **P**OP3 = **P**ick up on one device (server copy usually removed). **IMAP** = in all devices (server copy stays, everything syncs).

example.q: Which protocol lets you read the same mail on phone and laptop?
steps: The mail must stay on the server.
That is IMAP.

tricks.title: At sign
tricks.body: In ray@gmail.com the @ separates who from where: user at domain. An option with no @, or with a space or comma, is wrong.

example.q: Which character separates the username from the domain in an e-mail address?
steps: The character reads as 'at'.

mistakes.wrong: Saying CC receivers are hidden.
mistakes.right: BCC is hidden. CC is fully visible.

mistakes.wrong: Making SMTP the receiving protocol.
mistakes.right: SMTP only sends. POP3 and IMAP receive.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking Reply All reaches the hidden BCC list.
mistakes.right: Reply All reaches the sender and the To and CC people. BCC stays hidden.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking POP3 keeps mail synced on many devices.
mistakes.right: IMAP does that. POP3 downloads to one device.

mistakes.wrong: Using Reply when the whole group must see your answer.
mistakes.right: Reply goes only to the sender. Use Reply All for everyone.

subtopics.notes:
### What e-mail is
**E-mail (electronic mail)** sends messages between accounts on **mail servers**.

An address has two parts joined by **@** (read "at"): username, then domain. Take ray.kiran@gmail.com.

- **ray.kiran** is the username.
- **gmail.com** is the domain, the mail service.

Gmail, Outlook and Yahoo Mail are mail services.

### Fields of a new mail
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **To** | The main receivers |
| **CC** (Carbon Copy) | Extra receivers. Everyone sees all To and CC addresses. |
| **BCC** (Blind Carbon Copy) | Hidden receivers. To and CC people cannot see them. |
| **Subject** | A one-line summary |
| **Attachment** | A file sent along, shown by a paperclip. Size is limited. |
| **Signature** | A fixed sign-off block |

> **Rule:** CC is visible to all. BCC is hidden from the To and CC receivers. Use BCC for mass mails to protect addresses.

If a mail was sent to a hidden BCC list, Reply All reaches only the sender.

### The three protocols
| Protocol | Job | How it works |
|---|---|---|
| **SMTP** (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), port 25 | Sends mail | Pushes mail from client to server, and between servers |
| **POP3** (Post Office Protocol v3), port 110 | Receives mail | Downloads to one device, usually removing it from the server |
| **IMAP** (Internet Message Access Protocol), port 143 | Receives mail | Mail stays on the server and syncs on all devices |

**MIME** (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) lets e-mail carry attachments, images and non-English text.

> **Tip:** SMTP Sends. POP Picks up on one device. IMAP is In sync everywhere.

### Mail actions
- **Compose** writes a new mail. **Send** sends it.
- **Reply** answers only the sender.
- **Reply All** answers the sender and everyone in To and CC.
- **Forward** passes the mail to new people.

### Mail folders
| Folder | Holds |
|---|---|
| Inbox | Received mail |
| Outbox | Mail waiting to be sent |
| Sent | Mail already sent |
| Drafts | Unfinished mail |
| Spam or Junk | Mail the filter marked as junk |
| Trash or Bin | Deleted mail |

Never click links in spam.

### The journey of one mail
1. You press Send. Your mail server uses **SMTP** to push the mail to the server named after the @ domain.
2. The receiver's server keeps it in her mailbox.
3. Her app fetches it with **IMAP** or **POP3**.

**Webmail** is a mail service used in a browser, like Gmail. A **mail client** is an installed app, like Outlook or Thunderbird. **Filters and labels** sort mail automatically. **Autoresponders** reply for you when you are away.

patterns.name: CC/BCC visibility scenario
patterns.howToSpot: A sending scenario asks who can see whom, or which field to use so receivers do not see each other.
steps: CC receivers are visible to everyone.
BCC receivers are hidden from To and CC people.
BCC receivers do not see each other either.
Use BCC for bulk mails to protect addresses.
patterns.why: The hidden list stays hidden even when someone replies.

example.q: Ravi sends a mail to 200 customers with all addresses in BCC. If a customer presses Reply All, the reply goes to:
steps: BCC addresses are hidden from the other receivers.
So Reply All has only the sender to answer.

patterns.name: Protocol direction: SMTP vs POP3 vs IMAP
patterns.howToSpot: 'Protocol used to SEND e-mail', 'downloads mail to one device', 'keeps mail synced on the server'.
steps: Sending means SMTP.
Downloading to one device means POP3.
Staying on the server and syncing means IMAP.
Reject options with the roles reversed.
patterns.why: Each protocol has one direction, and options swap them.

example.q: Which protocol is used to SEND an e-mail from the client to the mail server?
steps: Sending is done by one protocol only.
POP3 and IMAP only fetch incoming mail.

patterns.name: E-mail address and fields anatomy
patterns.howToSpot: 'In rani@gmail.com, the part before @ is', 'what separates user and domain', or naming Subject, Attachment or Signature.
steps: Split the address at @.
Before @ is the username.
After @ is the domain.
Match the field to its plain meaning.
patterns.why: The @ is the only separator.

example.q: In the address kiran.verma@yahoo.in, the username is:
steps: Split at the @ sign.
The part before it is the username.

patterns.name: Reply, Reply All, Forward, Spam, Draft
patterns.howToSpot: A scenario about who receives your answer, or the meaning of spam, draft or forward.
steps: Reply goes to the sender only.
Reply All goes to the sender and all in To and CC.
Forward passes the mail to new receivers.
A draft is written but not sent.
patterns.why: Choose the action by who must read your answer.

example.q: Swati received a circular sent to her whole class. She wants only the teacher to read her answer. She should use:
steps: The teacher is the sender.
Only Reply goes to the sender alone.

patterns.name: Mail folders
patterns.howToSpot: 'Unsent mail is kept in', 'mail waiting to be sent is in', 'junk mail goes to'.
steps: Received mail is in the Inbox.
Waiting to be sent is the Outbox.
Unfinished mail is in Drafts.
Filtered junk is in Spam.
patterns.why: Each folder holds one state of a mail.

example.q: A mail that was written but not sent is found in the:
steps: Not sent and not finished means it is saved as a draft.
Drafts holds such mail.

patterns.name: MIME and port numbers
patterns.howToSpot: 'Standard that allows attachments and images', or 'default port of SMTP, POP3 or IMAP'.
steps: Attachments, images and non-English text point to MIME.
Recall the ports: SMTP 25, POP3 110, IMAP 143.
Match each protocol to its own port.
patterns.why: Three numbers and one full form cover this pattern.

example.q: The default port number of POP3 is:
steps: SMTP is 25.
POP3 is 110.
IMAP is 143.

revision: Address = username @ domain. The @ separates the two.
CC is visible to all. BCC is hidden from To and CC receivers.
SMTP sends (port 25). POP3 downloads to one device (port 110). IMAP syncs everywhere (port 143).
Reply = sender only. Reply All = sender plus To and CC. Forward = new receivers.
Folders: Inbox, Outbox, Sent, Drafts, Spam, Trash.
MIME lets e-mail carry attachments, images and non-English text.

subtopics.title: e-Banking and digital payments
subtopics.concept: **e-Banking** means banking through the bank's secure website or app. **NEFT** settles in batches with no minimum. **RTGS** is real time with a minimum of Rs. 2 lakh. **IMPS** and **UPI** are instant and run 24x7. Banks never ask for your PIN, OTP or password.

tricks.title: NEFT vs RTGS
tricks.body: **RTGS** is real time, one by one, for large sums: minimum Rs. 2 lakh. **NEFT** settles in half-hourly batches, for any amount.

example.q: What is the minimum amount for RTGS?
steps: RTGS is meant for large transfers.
The floor is 2 lakh.

tricks.title: IFSC is 11
tricks.body: IFSC has **11 characters**: 4 letters for the bank, a zero, then 6 characters for the branch. MICR is the 9-digit cheque strip.

example.q: How many characters does an IFSC code have?
steps: 4 for the bank, 1 zero, 6 for the branch.

tricks.title: 2FA needs two keys
tricks.body: Two-factor means a password (you know) plus an OTP or fingerprint (you have or are). One stolen password is not enough.

example.q: Entering a password and then an SMS OTP is an example of:
steps: Password is one factor.
The OTP is a second factor.

mistakes.wrong: Giving NEFT the 2 lakh minimum.
mistakes.right: RTGS has the minimum. NEFT has none.

mistakes.wrong: Saying IMPS works only for foreign banks.
mistakes.right: IMPS is an Indian instant payment service, 24x7.

mistakes.wrong: Sharing an OTP with a caller who says he is from the bank.
mistakes.right: Real banks never ask. Refuse and disconnect.

mistakes.wrong: Counting IFSC as 9 characters.
mistakes.right: IFSC has 11 characters. MICR has 9 digits.

mistakes.wrong: Confusing CVV with PIN.
mistakes.right: CVV is the 3 digits on the card back. PIN is your secret number.

subtopics.notes:
### Banking from a distance
**e-Banking (net banking)** is banking through the bank's secure **website**. **Mobile banking** uses the bank's **app**.

An **ATM (Automated Teller Machine)** gives cash, balance enquiry, a mini statement and PIN change.

All of them work by sending instructions over secure networks, not paper slips.

### Money-transfer systems of India
**NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India)** was set up in 2008. It runs most retail payment systems.

| System | Full form | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **NEFT** | National Electronic Funds Transfer | Settles in batches (half-hourly). No minimum. 24x7 since December 2019. |
| **RTGS** | Real Time Gross Settlement | Real time, one transfer at a time. **Minimum Rs. 2 lakh.** 24x7 since December 2020. |
| **IMPS** | Immediate Payment Service | Instant, 24x7, through mobile or internet banking. |
| **UPI** | Unified Payments Interface (2016) | Instant app-to-app transfer. 24x7. |

> **Watch:** The 2 lakh minimum belongs to RTGS. NEFT has no minimum.

### Which system to pick
Ask two questions. Is the amount large? Must it move at once?

| Need | System |
|---|---|
| Any amount, batch settlement is fine | NEFT |
| Large amount (Rs. 2 lakh or more), real time | RTGS |
| Instant, through mobile or internet banking | IMPS |
| Instant, using a VPA or QR | UPI |

> **Example:** Sending Rs. 5,00,000 in real time is an RTGS job. Sending Rs. 500 to a friend by QR is UPI.

### UPI in short
- UPI uses a **VPA** (virtual payment address) in the form name@bank.
- You can also pay by **QR** code.
- **BHIM** is one UPI app.
- NPCI built UPI.

### Bank codes
| Code | Size | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **IFSC** (Indian Financial System Code) | **11 characters** | Identifies the bank branch |
| **MICR** (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) | **9 digits** | Cheque strip that speeds clearing |
| **SWIFT** | Not asked | Code for international transfers |

An IFSC such as SBIN0001234 has three parts. SBIN is the bank (4 letters). Then comes 0. Then 001234 is the branch (6 characters).

### PIN, CVV, OTP and two factors
- **PIN** is your secret number at an ATM or UPI app.
- **CVV** is the 3-digit Card Verification Value on the back of the card.
- **OTP** is a One Time Password. It works for one login or one payment only.
- **Two-factor authentication (2FA)** needs two proofs: something you know (password) and something you have or are (OTP, fingerprint).

One stolen password is not enough. That is the point of 2FA.

### Safe habits
- Banks **never ask** for PIN, OTP, CVV or password by call, SMS or mail. The caller is a fraudster.
- Check HTTPS and the padlock before you pay.
- Avoid public Wi-Fi for transactions.
- Unknown links are phishing. Do not tap them.
- Report cyber-fraud on the national helpline **1930**.

> **Tip:** If anyone asks for your OTP, refuse. No real bank needs it from you.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Full form of HTTP/HTML/URL/ISP/SMTP/ATM/IFSC/OTP' or a wrongly matched pair where one word of an expansion is changed.
pyqPatterns.approach: Expand letter by letter from family tables: web family (HTTP, HTML, URL, WWW), mail family (SMTP, POP3, IMAP, e-mail @), banking family (NEFT, RTGS, UPI, NPCI, IFSC, MICR, OTP, CVV, PIN, ATM). The planted error is one swapped word, e.g. 'Hyper Transfer Markup Language' for HTML.

example.q: The full form of SMTP is:
example.solution: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol — the sending protocol of e-mail.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a browser?' with Google planted among Chrome/Firefox, or 'which is a search engine?' with Chrome planted among Bing/Yahoo.
pyqPatterns.approach: Browsers are programs installed on your device (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, Opera); search engines are websites reached through them (Google, Bing, Yahoo, DuckDuckGo). The famous trap: Google called a browser, or Chrome called a search engine.

example.q: Which of the following is a web browser?
example.solution: Chrome — the program that shows pages; Google is the search engine inside it.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A mail scenario: who can see whose address, what Reply All reaches, or which field protects a bulk list of receivers.
pyqPatterns.approach: CC is a visible copy (everyone in To/CC sees all those addresses); BCC is blind (To/CC never see the BCC list, and BCC receivers are hidden from each other). Bulk mails to strangers go in BCC; Reply All on a BCC'd mail reaches only the sender.

example.q: A mail to 200 customers uses BCC for all addresses. Reply All by one customer reaches:
example.solution: Only the sender — the BCC list stays hidden.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Protocol used to send e-mail', 'which protocol syncs mail across devices', 'protocol that moves web pages', 'protocol of file transfer' — directions matched.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix the map: SMTP sends mail; POP3 downloads to one device; IMAP syncs on the server; HTTP/HTTPS move web pages (443 = secure); FTP transfers files; DHCP assigns IPs; DNS resolves names. Sending questions always answer SMTP.

example.q: Which protocol is used to send e-mail from a client to the mail server?
example.solution: SMTP — Simple Mail Transfer Protocol; POP3 and IMAP only receive.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Minimum of 2 lakh belongs to which system?', 'which is instant 24x7', 'full form of NEFT/RTGS/UPI', 'UPI is run by ___' — the rails mixed in options.
pyqPatterns.approach: NEFT = batch transfers, no minimum; RTGS = real-time, transaction-wise, minimum 2,00,000 rupees; IMPS = instant inside banking apps; UPI = instant by UPI ID/QR, built by NPCI. The recurring trap gives NEFT the 2-lakh floor that belongs to RTGS.

example.q: A transfer of 5,00,000 rupees is needed immediately, transaction by transaction. Which system fits?
example.solution: RTGS — real-time gross settlement, designed for high-value transfers (minimum 2 lakh).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A URL is printed and a part is asked: protocol, domain, country code or path; or the full form of URL.
pyqPatterns.approach: Split at slashes: protocol (https://) + domain (www.site.in) + path (/folder/page.html). Country codes: .in India, .uk UK; generic: .com, .org, .gov, .edu. DNS converts the whole domain to an IP address.

example.q: In https://www.mysite.in/exams/ssc.html, 'www.mysite.in' is the:
example.solution: Domain name — https is the protocol; /exams/ssc.html is the path.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which code has 11 characters', 'the 9-digit cheque code', 'the 3-digit number on the card', 'which code for international transfers'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Line them up: IFSC = 11 characters (4 bank letters + 0 + 6 branch) for domestic transfers; MICR = 9 digits on the cheque strip; CVV = 3 digits on the card back; PIN = your secret at machines; OTP = one-time password; SWIFT = international transfers.

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following is a web browser?
solvedExamples.solution: Microsoft Edge is browser software that displays web pages. Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo are search engines - websites that index the web.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Installed program = browser; website you search inside = engine. Edge/Chrome/Firefox/Safari/Opera are the usual browser options.

solvedExamples.q: An e-mail is sent with the addresses of four colleagues placed in the BCC field. Which statement is correct?
options: All four can see each other's addresses
The To recipients can see the BCC addresses
The four receive copies whose addresses are hidden from other recipients
BCC recipients do not receive attachments
solvedExamples.solution: Blind Carbon Copy hides its recipient list: each BCC recipient gets the full mail (including attachments), but To/CC recipients cannot see who was blind-copied.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 'Blind' = nobody sees the list. The mail itself (with attachments) still arrives.

solvedExamples.q: Which protocol is used to SEND e-mail from a client to a mail server?
solvedExamples.solution: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) handles outgoing mail. POP3 and IMAP fetch incoming mail (POP3 downloads, IMAP syncs), and HTTP serves web pages.
solvedExamples.shortcut: S in SMTP = Send; the receiving protocols are POP3/IMAP.

solvedExamples.q: Match: (a) NEFT (b) RTGS (c) UPI with (i) instant app-based transfer via VPA (ii) batch settlement, no minimum (iii) real-time gross settlement, minimum Rs. 2 lakh
solvedExamples.solution: NEFT settles in half-hourly batches with no minimum amount (a-ii); RTGS settles each transaction individually in real time with a Rs. 2-lakh floor (b-iii); UPI is the instant VPA/QR app rail run by NPCI (c-i).
solvedExamples.shortcut: RTGS grabs the 2-lakh rule; NEFT is the batch rail; UPI is the phone-first instant one.

practice.q: The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 by:
practice.solution: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the WWW at CERN in 1989 and wrote the first browser. Vint Cerf co-designed TCP/IP; Larry Page co-founded Google.
practice.shortcut: Web = Berners-Lee, 1989, CERN. Internet (1970s TCP/IP) = Cerf and Kahn.

practice.q: ARPANET, the precursor of today's Internet, was launched in:
practice.solution: ARPANET went live in 1969 connecting UCLA and Stanford Research Institute, funded by the US Department of Defense.
practice.shortcut: ARPANET 1969 - the 60s birth of the network.

practice.q: The service that translates a domain name like www.ssc.gov.in into an IP address is:
practice.solution: DNS (Domain Name System) resolves human-friendly names to numeric IP addresses. DHCP assigns IP addresses automatically; FTP transfers files; the ISP is your access provider.
practice.shortcut: DNS = the Internet's phonebook: name in, number out.

practice.q: In the URL https://www.ssc.gov.in, the component '.in' is the:
practice.solution: .in is the country-code top-level domain for India. 'https' is the protocol, 'www' the sub-domain/host, 'ssc' the registered domain name.
practice.shortcut: Read right to left: .in = TLD, .gov = second level, ssc = the name.

practice.q: Which of the following is NOT a web browser?
practice.solution: Yahoo is a web portal/search engine, not browser software. Opera, Safari and Firefox are browsers.
practice.shortcut: Scan for the service/brand that you cannot install as a program - that is the odd one.

practice.q: Receiving a file from a web server to your computer is called:
practice.solution: Downloading copies data from the server down to your device; uploading sends it the other way; streaming plays without saving the whole file.
practice.shortcut: Down to you = download; up to the server = upload.

practice.q: The browser shortcut to open a new tab is:
practice.solution: Ctrl+T opens a new tab; Ctrl+N a new window; Ctrl+W closes the current tab; Ctrl+Tab cycles through open tabs.
practice.shortcut: T = Tab, N = window. Ctrl+W wipes the tab.

practice.q: The standard that allows e-mails to carry attachments such as images and documents is:
practice.solution: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) extends e-mail to carry multimedia, attachments and non-ASCII text. SMTP is the transport protocol for mail.

practice.q: In an e-mail address kiran.ray@nic.in, the part before @ is the:
practice.solution: The format is username@domain: 'kiran.ray' is the user's mailbox name on the domain 'nic.in'.
practice.shortcut: Who@where - the left side is the person.

practice.q: Which e-mail protocol keeps messages on the server so that the same mailbox stays in sync across a phone, tablet and laptop?
practice.solution: IMAP stores mail on the server and synchronises state across devices. POP3 traditionally downloads and removes mail (single-device model), SMTP sends, FTP moves files.

practice.q: The minimum amount that can be transferred through RTGS is:
practice.solution: RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) is meant for large-value transfers - the floor is Rs. 2 lakh, settled individually and instantly. NEFT carries smaller amounts in batches with no minimum.

practice.q: UPI, the instant real-time payment system, is developed and operated by:
practice.solution: UPI (2016) is built and operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), the umbrella organisation for retail payments (it also runs IMPS, RuPay, BHIM). RBI regulates but does not operate UPI.
practice.shortcut: NPCI runs the retail rails: UPI, IMPS, RuPay, AePS. RBI is the regulator.

practice.q: An IFSC code used in electronic fund transfers contains how many characters?
practice.solution: The Indian Financial System Code is 11 characters: 4 letters for the bank, a zero, and 6 characters identifying the branch (e.g. SBIN0007245).

practice.q: Small text files a website stores in your browser to remember sessions and preferences are called:
practice.solution: Cookies hold site-specific data (login sessions, carts, preferences, tracking IDs). They are plain text files - not programs and not viruses.

practice.q: The keyboard shortcut to bookmark (favourite) the current page in all major browsers is:
practice.solution: Ctrl+D adds the current page to bookmarks/favourites. (Ctrl+B is bold in Office; in some browsers it toggles the bookmarks BAR, which is why the safe exam answer for bookmarking a page is Ctrl+D.)

practice.q: The Internet is best described as a —
options: Global network of interconnected computer networks
practice.solution: The Internet is a **network of networks** — no single owner, no single computer.

practice.q: The World Wide Web (WWW) and the Internet are —
options: Two names of the same thing
Different: WWW is a service that runs on the Internet
Different: the Internet runs on the WWW
practice.solution: **Internet = the infrastructure; WWW = hyperlinked pages carried on it** — along with e-mail, FTP and other services.
practice.shortcut: Road system vs traffic on it.

practice.q: ARPANET, the ancestor of the Internet, was launched in —
practice.solution: **ARPANET, 1969** — a US Defence project. 1989 is the WWW's year.

practice.q: Which service does NOT run on the Internet?
practice.solution: E-mail, FTP and VoIP are all Internet services; **punch cards are 1960s input media**, older than the networks.

practice.q: URL stands for —
practice.solution: **URL = Uniform Resource Locator** — the address of a web resource.

practice.q: In the URL https://www.gov.in/schemes/2026.html, the part '/schemes/2026.html' is the —
options: Path to the page on the server
practice.solution: https = protocol, www.gov.in = domain, and everything after is the **path** to the exact file.

practice.q: The '.in' ending of a domain name indicates —
practice.solution: .in is **India's country code**; .com is commercial, .org organisation, .gov government, .edu education.

practice.q: DNS translates —
options: IP addresses into domain names only
practice.solution: **DNS = the Internet's phonebook**: you give a name, it returns the numeric IP the machines use.

practice.q: Which server ASSIGNS an IP address to a device joining a network?
practice.solution: **DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) assigns IPs**; DNS only translates names — the classic swap.

practice.q: The company that provides your Internet connection is called an —
practice.solution: **ISP = Internet Service Provider** (Jio, Airtel, BSNL).

practice.q: HTTP stands for —
practice.solution: **HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol** — the rules for moving web pages; HTTPS is its secure version.

practice.q: Which pair is wrongly matched?
practice.solution: HTML = **HyperText Markup Language** — 'Hyper Transfer' is the planted error.

practice.q: Which of the following is a search engine?
practice.solution: **Google indexes and finds pages** — a search engine. Chrome, Firefox and Safari are browsers.

practice.q: Which option lists ONLY web browsers?
practice.solution: All three are browser programs. Option B lists search engines, C lists e-mail services, D lists programming languages.

practice.q: Ctrl+T in a browser opens —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+T = new Tab** (T for tab); Ctrl+N opens a new window.

practice.q: Which shortcut opens the BROWSING HISTORY panel?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+H = History**; Ctrl+J opens the downloads list — the standard trap pair.

practice.q: In Chrome, an incognito window opens with —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Shift+N** opens Incognito in Chrome; plain Ctrl+N is a normal new window.

practice.q: Match: 1. Ctrl+D 2. Ctrl+F 3. Ctrl+J — a. find on page b. bookmark c. downloads
practice.solution: Ctrl+**D**rops a bookmark, Ctrl+**F**inds on the page, Ctrl+**J** opens downloads.
practice.shortcut: D bookmark, F find, J downloads.

practice.q: Sending a file from your computer to a web server is —
practice.solution: **Upload = you to server; download = server to you.**

practice.q: The browser cache exists mainly to —
options: Speed up revisits by storing copies of pages
practice.solution: **Cache = local copies** of pages and images, so a second visit loads without refetching everything.

practice.q: Which statement about cookies is TRUE?
options: They are viruses that damage files
They are programs that run in background
They are small text files a website stores on your device
They store the pages for offline use
practice.solution: **Cookies = passive text files** (logins, preferences, tracking) — a privacy topic, never a virus.

practice.q: Private (incognito) browsing on a shared computer mainly ensures that —
options: The ISP cannot see your activity
Websites cannot see your visit at all
History and cookies of that session are deleted when the window closes
practice.solution: Incognito forgets **locally** — websites and the ISP still see the traffic.

practice.q: Which action does NOT need an Internet connection?
options: Reading a page saved earlier from the cache/Offline
practice.solution: Only the locally saved copy can be read offline; sending, searching and downloading all need the net.

practice.q: Watching a video as it arrives, without saving the whole file first, is —
practice.solution: **Streaming plays while the data flows in** — the file need not be stored first.

practice.q: In an e-mail, CC stands for —
practice.solution: **CC = Carbon Copy** — a visible duplicate to extra receivers; BCC = Blind Carbon Copy.

practice.q: Receivers in the To and CC fields —
practice.solution: **BCC is blind**: To/CC receivers never see those addresses; each BCC receiver doesn't see the others either.

practice.q: To mail 500 members of an association without exposing their addresses, use —
practice.solution: **BCC hides the list from everyone** — the standard bulk-mail etiquette.

practice.q: Which protocol is used to SEND e-mail?
practice.solution: **SMTP = Simple Mail Transfer Protocol** — it pushes mail out; POP3/IMAP only fetch.

practice.q: Which protocol downloads incoming mail to a single device, usually removing it from the server?
practice.solution: **POP3 = Post Office Protocol** — pick up the mail like a letter-box: one download, one device.
practice.shortcut: POP Picks it off the server.

practice.q: Meera reads her mail on her phone, tablet and laptop, and every device shows the same mailbox. Her account uses —
practice.solution: **IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs all devices**; POP3 would strand messages on one machine.

practice.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
practice.solution: SMTP sends; POP3 and IMAP receive; web pages travel by HTTP, not POP3.

practice.q: In the e-mail address ramesh.k@gmail.com, the part 'ramesh.k' is the —
practice.solution: **username @ domain** — ramesh.k is the user, gmail.com the mail service.

practice.q: The symbol that separates the username from the domain in an e-mail address is —
practice.solution: **@ means 'at'** — user at this service. It has been the e-mail separator since the 1970s.

practice.q: Which field of an e-mail carries the files clipped to the message?
practice.solution: **Attachments** (paperclip icon) carry files; Subject is the one-line summary; Signature is the sign-off.

practice.q: Unsolicited junk e-mail is called —
practice.solution: **Spam = junk mail**; the filter parks it in the Spam folder.

practice.q: A mail that is written but not yet sent is stored as a —
practice.solution: **Draft** = the waiting room of unsent mail.

practice.q: Reply All on a mail addressed to you and 40 classmates reaches —
options: The sender and everyone on To/CC
practice.solution: **Reply All = sender + To + CC list**; BCC members were never disclosed and stay out.

practice.q: NEFT stands for —
practice.solution: **NEFT = National Electronic Funds Transfer** — batch-wise transfers run by RBI.

practice.q: Which transfer system has a MINIMUM transaction of 2,00,000 rupees?
practice.solution: **RTGS = Real Time Gross Settlement** — built for high-value transfers; minimum 2 lakh. NEFT has no minimum.

practice.q: Which of these moves money INSTANTLY, 24x7, using just a UPI ID or QR code?
practice.solution: **UPI = Unified Payments Interface** — instant app-to-app transfer built by NPCI.

practice.q: Match: 1. NEFT 2. RTGS 3. UPI — a. batch transfers, no minimum b. real-time, minimum 2 lakh c. instant payments by NPCI
practice.solution: NEFT = batches (no minimum), RTGS = real-time with the 2-lakh floor, UPI = NPCI's instant rail.

practice.q: UPI is operated by —
practice.solution: **NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India)** built and runs UPI, IMPS, RuPay and NEFT systems.

practice.q: OTP stands for —
practice.solution: **OTP = One Time Password** — valid for one login or one transaction, for a short time.

practice.q: The 3-digit security number printed on the back of a debit/credit card is the —
practice.solution: **CVV = Card Verification Value** — never share it; it pairs with the card number for online payments.

practice.q: Login by password PLUS an OTP sent to your phone is an example of —
practice.solution: **2FA = two independent proofs** — something you know (password) plus something you receive or are (OTP, fingerprint).

practice.q: A caller claiming to be from your bank asks for the OTP you just received. The correct action is —
options: Share it to verify your account
Refuse and disconnect; banks never ask for OTPs
Send it by SMS for safety
practice.solution: No genuine bank asks for OTP, PIN, CVV or password — this is **vishing** (voice phishing).

practice.q: The secret number typed at the ATM along with the card is the —
practice.solution: **PIN = Personal Identification Number** — card + PIN authorise ATM transactions.

practice.q: An IFSC code contains how many characters?
practice.solution: **IFSC = 11 characters**: 4 letters of the bank + 0 + 6 characters of the branch (SBIN0001234).

practice.q: The 9-digit magnetic-ink code printed at the bottom of a cheque is the —
practice.solution: **MICR = Magnetic Ink Character Recognition** — 9 digits that speed up cheque clearing.

practice.q: For an international wire transfer to your account, the sender needs the —
practice.solution: **SWIFT codes identify banks worldwide** for cross-border transfers; IFSC works only inside India.

practice.q: In the IFSC code SBIN0001234, the first four letters identify the —
practice.solution: SBIN = State Bank of India; the 0 is a separator; **0001234 identifies the branch**.

practice.q: ATM stands for —
practice.solution: **ATM = Automated Teller Machine** — a 'teller' is the person behind the counter; the machine does that job.

practice.q: Which of these can NOT be done at a normal ATM?
options: Opening a new fixed deposit instantly
practice.solution: ATMs handle cash, balance, mini statements and PIN changes; **fixed deposits need the branch, app or net banking**.
practice.shortcut: ATM = cash point, not an FD desk.

practice.q: Banking done through the bank's official app on a phone is called —
practice.solution: **Net banking = website; mobile banking = app** — both run from the same account.
